name: Amalfi Cathedral
summary:
The Cathedral of Saint Andrew (Duomo di Sant'Andrea) in Amalfi, Italy, founded in the 9th century CE and expanded in the 10th-11th centuries in a remarkable Arab-Norman Romanesque style — a product of Amalfi's unique position as one of medieval Italy's most powerful maritime republics with close trading connections to the Arab world and the Byzantine Empire — is one of southern Italy's most architecturally distinctive churches. The Amalfi Cathedral's striped geometric facade and bronze doors (cast in Constantinople in 1065 CE) reflect the Mediterranean cosmopolitan culture of the Amalfitan Republic at its height.

The Amalfitan Republic (839-1137 CE) was one of the Italian Maritime Republics (with Venice, Genoa, and Pisa) — small city-states that dominated Mediterranean trade in the early medieval period. Amalfi was the wealthiest of the four in the 10th-11th centuries, with a population of 70,000 (larger than Milan at the time). The republic's merchants pioneered the magnetic compass's adoption in European navigation; Amalfi's 'Tabula Amalfitana' (10th-12th century maritime law code) was the foundation of Mediterranean maritime law.

The cathedral houses relics of Saint Andrew the Apostle (brought from Constantinople in 1208 CE after the Fourth Crusade's looting) — a relic that made Amalfi a major pilgrimage site. The Chiostro del Paradiso (Paradise Cloister, 1268 CE) — an exquisite interlaced Arab arches cloister — is one of southern Italy's most beautiful medieval spaces. Annual pilgrimage (June 27, Feast of Saint Andrew) continues to draw thousands.
